sections.summary: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, is led by the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days of testing by the devil, paralleling Israel's wilderness experience as God's 'son' but preparing to succeed where Israel failed.

The devil challenges Jesus to use his divine sonship for self-provision, and Jesus responds with Deuteronomy 8:3, trusting God's word rather than exercising power to meet his own need -- the lesson Israel failed to learn when they grumbled for food in the wilderness.

sections.section_title: The Second Test -- Authority over the Kingdoms
sections.summary: The devil offers Jesus immediate dominion over all kingdoms in exchange for worship, and Jesus responds with Deuteronomy 6:13, refusing to take a shortcut to the kingdom by giving to the devil what belongs only to God -- the test Israel failed when they turned to other gods.

sections.section_title: The Third Test -- The Temple Pinnacle
sections.summary: The devil quotes Psalm 91 to urge Jesus to force God to prove His faithfulness by throwing himself from the temple, and Jesus responds with Deuteronomy 6:16, refusing to test God as Israel did at Massah.
The devil departs after exhausting every category of temptation, but only 'until an opportune time,' signaling that the adversarial testing will return later in the narrative.
Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, teaches in synagogues, and is praised by all, establishing a positive initial reception that will be dramatically reversed in the next scene.

sections.section_title: Jesus in the Synagogue at Nazareth -- The Reading
sections.summary: Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1-2a in the Nazareth synagogue, deliberately stopping before 'the day of vengeance,' and declares 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing,' defining his mission as the inauguration of God's favor through good news, release, healing, and freedom.
The synagogue audience initially speaks well of Jesus but questions his credentials as Joseph's son, and Jesus preemptively invokes the principle that no prophet is welcome in his hometown.

Jesus cites the precedents of Elijah being sent to a Gentile widow in Sidon and Elisha healing Naaman the Syrian -- both instances where God directed His saving action to Gentiles when Israel proved unresponsive -- establishing the pattern that God's saving work moves to where it is received.

The Nazareth audience erupts in murderous rage at the implication that God's favor might extend beyond Israel to Gentiles, confirming the very pattern of prophetic rejection that Jesus described, while Jesus passes through their midst and leaves.
Jesus teaches in the Capernaum synagogue and the people are amazed at the authority of his message, contrasting with Nazareth's rejection.

Jesus casts out an unclean demon that recognizes him as 'the Holy One of God,' demonstrating the release of captives announced in the Isaiah 61 program, while silencing the demon's testimony about his identity.
Jesus rebukes a high fever afflicting Simon's mother-in-law with the same authoritative command used against demons, and she is immediately restored and begins serving them.
After the Sabbath ends, Jesus lays hands on each sick person individually, healing them all, while silencing the demons who identify him as the Son of God and the Christ.

Jesus withdraws to a secluded place, resists the crowds' desire to keep him, and declares that he must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to other cities because he was sent for this purpose, introducing the divine necessity that drives his mission.
